intro: Look at the dark stone rising before you. This is Diyarbakır Fortress, with the Hevsel Gardens at its feet, in Diyarbakır province. Its walls date from the 4th century AD: 5.8 kilometres of basalt, reckoned the longest unbroken defensive circuit after the Great Wall, wrapping around the Hevsel Gardens on the Tigris.
history: The walls took their present form under Rome in the fourth century AD. After that, one power after another repaired and extended them: Byzantines, Marwanids, Artuqids, Aq Qoyunlu and Ottomans. Built of black basalt, the circuit runs 5.8 kilometres, with 82 towers and four main gates. Now look closely at the towers. Their inscriptions and animal reliefs form a stone archive, in which every dynasty that held the city left its signature.
highlights: As you wander, don't miss the Ulu Beden Tower and the Seven Brothers Tower, then pass the Mardin Gate and the Urfa Gate. Look out over the Hevsel Gardens, and end at the Inner citadel.
facts: Did you know? The Hevsel Gardens below the walls have been farmed without a break for eight thousand years. They fed the city, and UNESCO inscribed them together with the walls as a single whole. The 5.8 kilometres of basalt are reckoned the longest unbroken defensive circuit in the world after the Great Wall. And the inscriptions on the towers carry the signature of every dynasty that held the city, from Rome to the Ottomans. This wall is an archive of power, written in stone.
outro: This brings our journey along Diyarbakır Fortress and the Hevsel Gardens to an end. Before you go, please leave the stones untouched, keep to the marked paths and carry water with you. These walls have stood for centuries; let them stand for those who come after you. Enjoy your visit.
